title: What happens after the bin
description: Your recycling goes on a journey of sorting machines, magnets, and second lives — a peek inside.

body.heading: The sorting journey
paragraphs: After collection, mixed recycling usually travels to a sorting facility. Machines and people separate it: magnets pull out steel, spinning screens sort cardboard and paper, and air jets and sensors help sort plastics by type.
That is why clean, dry, loose items matter — they are far easier for both machines and people to sort correctly and safely.

body.heading: Second lives
paragraphs: Sorted materials become new products: aluminium cans can return as cans remarkably quickly, glass can be recycled again and again, and paper fibres can be reused several times before they wear out.
Recycling saves energy compared with making many materials from scratch — aluminium recycling is a famous example, using far less energy than producing new aluminium.

body.heading: Why reducing still wins
paragraphs: Even good recycling uses transport and energy. That is why the order matters: reduce first, reuse next, and recycle what remains. Your bin is the last step, not the first.

takeaway: Recycling sorts and remakes materials — valuable, but reducing and reusing come first.
